title: The Titanic
objective: After this level you can explain why the Titanic sank.
summary: Despite ice warnings, the Titanic kept its speed, struck an iceberg at 11:40 pm on April 14, 1912, and flooded at least five compartments, one too many. It sank at 2:20 am.

cards.headline: Many claimed the Titanic couldn't sink. It sank on its first voyage.
cards.body: It left Southampton, England, for New York on April 10, 1912, and never arrived. Forget the legends: here's what actually went wrong, hour by hour and compartment by compartment.

events.label: Iceberg warnings arrive all day; the course shifts south, but the speed stays up
Water is reported in at least five compartments
The stern slips under, and the ship is gone

cards.headline: One compartment too many
cards.body: The Titanic's hull was split into watertight compartments, and it could stay afloat with four of them flooded. That's why many claimed it was unsinkable. But the iceberg left a series of thin gashes in the hull, and water poured into at least five. Remember Level 73: about 90% of an iceberg sits underwater, so most of what a ship can hit is out of sight.

cards.headline: Too few boats, and a patrol
cards.body: The 20 lifeboats had room for only 1,178 people, and more than 2,200 were aboard. More than 1,500 died. The disaster pushed governments into the first Safety of Life at Sea convention in 1914, which set up the International Ice Patrol to watch the North Atlantic for icebergs, many of them from Level 73's Greenland glaciers. It's still on watch today.

cards.headline: The Titanic: explained
learned: Ice warnings arrived, but the speed stayed up
It struck an iceberg at 11:40 PM on April 14, 1912
At least five compartments flooded; it could survive four
Result: SOLAS in 1914 and the Ice Patrol

questions.prompt: The Titanic could stay afloat with four compartments flooded. How many did the iceberg let water into?

options.label: One
options.rationale: The damage ran along the hull, across several compartments.

options.label: Three
options.rationale: That would have left it afloat.

options.label: All of them at once
options.rationale: Water reached at least five, one more than it could survive.

questions.explanation: Water poured into at least five compartments, one more than the Titanic could survive.

questions.prompt: Why did so many people die when the Titanic sank?

options.label: It sank within ten minutes of the collision
options.rationale: It struck at 11:40 PM and sank at 2:20 AM.

options.label: Nobody on board knew about icebergs in the area
Its lifeboats had room for only about half aboard
The ship was far from any shipping lane
options.rationale: The problem was the lifeboats, not the location.

questions.explanation: The 20 lifeboats held only 1,178 people, but more than 2,200 were aboard; more than 1,500 died.

questions.prompt: Which Level 32 episode best matches how the Titanic handled the ice warnings of April 14, 1912?

options.label: Whalers using a current they already knew about
options.rationale: The whalers acted on what they knew; the Titanic kept its speed.

options.label: Mail captains ignoring Franklin's Gulf Stream chart
Franklin asking a Nantucket captain why the mail was so slow
options.rationale: That was asking for advice, not ignoring it.

options.label: Westerly winds carrying the Gulf Stream's warmth to Europe
options.rationale: That's the current's effect on climate, not a sailor's choice.

questions.explanation: The mail captains seem to have ignored the chart they were given, and the Titanic kept its speed up through a day of iceberg warnings.
